facts.claim: Most studies did not support the idea that active social media use leads to higher well-being while passive social media use leads to lower well-being.
facts.quote: Most studies did not support the hypothesized associations of ASMU and PSMU with well-/ill-being.
facts.causalWarning: causal wording, but the cited study only shows an association

facts.claim: Most of the results regarding the link between active or passive social media use and mental health were negligible, with an effect size of less than .10.
facts.quote: Most ESs were negligible (|r| < .10), with the exception of between-person associations for active SMU and greater online support (r = .34), wellbeing (r = .15), positive affect (r = .11), and symptoms of anxiety (r = .12), and passive SMU and greater online support (r = .15).

facts.claim: Active social media use is linked to a negative relationship with appearance valence in physically active men.
facts.quote: Results showed a negative relationship between active social media use and appearance valence.

facts.claim: Time spent on active or passive social media use may be too coarse to lead to meaningful associations with well-being or ill-being.
facts.quote: Time spent on ASMU and PSMU may be too coarse to lead to meaningful associations with well-/ill-being.
facts.causalWarning: causal wording, but the cited study only shows an association

facts.claim: Passive social media use is linked to worse emotional outcomes in general social media contexts, but not in social media groups.
facts.quote: Moderator analyses revealed that passive use was associated with worse emotional outcomes in general SM contexts, but not in the context of SM groups.

facts.claim: Passive social media use is linked to higher appearance salience and drive for muscularity in physically active men.
facts.quote: Passive social media use was predictive of higher appearance salience and drive for muscularity in linear regression models.

research.angle: While passive use is linked to worse emotional outcomes in general contexts and higher appearance salience in some men, many studies fail to find a significant link between active or passive use and well-being.
research.verdict: The evidence is mixed and often negligible, showing that the impact of social media use depends heavily on the specific context and the type of content rather than just the mode of engagement.
research.caveat: Many studies used 'time spent' as a metric, which may be too broad to provide meaningful insights into psychological outcomes.
